Where this week's projections come from

Each player's number blends, where he has one from each:

  • our model and ESPN's projection, 46% and 54%, measured on 2067 graded games;
  • the betting market's implied points, 32% where books price him -- none in this week's numbers yet: books post a game's props a day or two before kickoff, the Sunday-morning run buys them, and a refresh spends no credits, so it uses only props already bought;
  • the FantasyPros consensus projection, 13% (12 of your 14 players), measured on 1676 graded games.

Each weight is the one that would have been most accurate on this season's finished games, pulled toward its starting value until enough are graded. The same numbers set the lineup, P(win), this week's pickups and streams, and this week's part of every title-odds number on the page: waiver adds and drops, trades, the roster. Season values move 51% of the way toward the FantasyPros rest-of-season consensus (measured on 1423 graded games), and every season-long number uses them.

Consensus projections and rankings: analysis based on data from FantasyPros.

Title: points of your title odds lost without him, his spot filled from the wire, on the same seasons the hub prices every move on (grey: inside the noise). Mkt: what other managers see him worth a game; green above ours (sell), red below (hold).

Waivers tonight

Your waiver priority is 8 of 10. A claim that succeeds sends you to the back of the list, so the claims below are in order of what they are worth: the first that lands uses your priority.

Nothing to claim tonight: no pickup raises your title odds enough to be worth a move. Anything you have already entered is a claim the numbers below do not back.

Waiver moves, by title odds

Each pickup is priced in P(win the title) on the same simulated seasons: claiming now, against waiting and claiming only if he breaks out (you win that claim when your priority beats the other managers who also want him), less what your waiver priority is worth on future claims. Passing is not free: if he breaks out, a rival claims him, and what that does to your title odds is counted. Each move is priced on its own; make one, then refresh. Assumes about a third of active managers chase any one breakout. Injured free agents are priced as IR stashes: no roster spot until he is back, with the chance he never is.

Waiver plans: several moves together

Moves interact -- two backs chasing one lineup spot are worth less together, two dead roster spots turned into a starter and his handcuff can be worth more -- so every combination of two or three pickups and drops is screened, and the best priced in title odds against standing pat and against the best single move. Make the plan when it beats that single move by more than the simulation noise; a close call when by less.

No plan beats the best single move; make that one and refresh.

Pickups for this matchup

Every free agent who could start for you this week, added to your roster with your best lineup rebuilt around him and scored against your opponent on the same simulated games as your lineup as it stands -- the chance you win this week with him, against without. The title columns are the whole move in points of P(title), on the season simulation: Wk is this week's win -- the P(win) gain times what this game swings your title odds; Rest is every week after, his value less that of the player you drop; Net is the two together, less the waiver priority a claim spends. The verdict goes on Net: a pickup that wins this week can still cost more later than it gains now. If he is on waivers, the claim has to clear before his game.

Could be worth is his ceiling a game in a month if things break his way (85th percentile of how projections move). Worth a bench spot you would otherwise waste.

Trades

Trades close today (Nov 11). After that only waiver moves can change your roster.

Every 1-for-1, 2-for-1 and 1-for-2 with every team, and 2-for-2 among each side's eight most valuable players; when a deal frees one of your roster spots, the free agent who adds most fills it and is priced in. For you: priced in title odds for both teams on the same simulated seasons as the waiver moves. For him: he cannot see this tool, so his side is judged the way the market values players -- the platform's projection, a player's name and last season, this season so far, injuries -- in the proportions measured from Yahoo's rostership, plus whether he gets the best player in the deal and how active he is. The yes-chance ranks offers; it is a rough estimate, not a measured rate. Each trade is priced on its own, as an alternative to the others. The numbers are from a second, larger simulation than the one that picked the trades, so the pick does not flatter them; ± is the range that simulation's own noise leaves (95%), and a trade inside it is marked toss-up.

By expected gain: the chance he says yes times the title odds you gain.

Betting

Prop lines that look wrong. For each player and stat, the other books' quotes (their margin taken out; Pinnacle, the sharpest, counts double) are fitted to one curve of his outcomes, so any line can be priced: a book at 30.5 rushing yards when the rest sit near 72 shows as a near-certain over. Ours is the chance from our own projection of that stat and how much such projections miss by (2021-2025). Combined leans toward the books on yards (they know the matchup) and toward ours where we have been as good. EV is the expected profit per unit staked at that price: on the books' chance, and on the combined one. Way off: 10%+ on both the books' read and ours. One-sided markets (anytime touchdown) are left out.

Built Wed 10:29 AM ET. Age is how long before that each price was last read from its feed: the feeds are re-read every few hours (one of them mostly on Sunday, Tuesday and Wednesday mornings), not every refresh, and a price more than 90 minutes behind the newest for the same player, or more than 8 hours old, is left out as stale. Props move fast, so check the book before betting. Books limit accounts that keep taking prices well off the market.

Recommended: prices the other books say are wrong

Each one pays more than the other books' read says it should, and more than the combined read does: positive expected profit if the other books are right and the price is still there. Whether that has held is the record below (wins and losses, and whether the market then moved toward these bets or away from them); until it does, keep stakes small. Even a real edge loses most single bets.

None right now: no price beats what the other books say by 2%+ (14 sides priced). Lines that are way off are rare and get fixed fast; the board checks every refresh.

Where only our projection disagrees (not recommended)

The books agree with each other here and our per-stat projection does not; on the books' read these lose money, so they are leans, not bets. Unproven: our edge over the market has three weeks behind it, so these are graded separately below before they mean anything.

The close is the early test of an edge: a real one beats the closing price more often than not, and the market moves toward it. Overall: 31% of 368 beat the closing price; the market moved toward 33% and away from 44% (average -0.1 points).

  • Books' read: 54 flagged, 25-24, -0.7 units; 57% of 54 beat the closing price; the market moved toward 18% and away from 64% (average -1.9 points)
  • Our projection only: 315 flagged, 163-123, +30.6 units; 27% of 314 beat the closing price; the market moved toward 35% and away from 41% (average +0.2 points)

Parlays

Two or three of the recommended bets above, at the same book and from different games (so they don't move together). A parlay pays the legs' odds multiplied and wins only if all do, so a parlay of good prices multiplies the edge — and the error in the chances, and the book's margin on any leg that isn't an edge. It wins far less often, so keep the stake smaller than a single bet's. Legs avg is what the same legs earn as separate bets.

None right now: it needs two recommended bets at one book from different games.

Hedging: sure bets

The same line at two books, over at one and under at the other, where the two prices together pay more than the stakes whichever way it lands. Stake the split shown. They are rare and corrected in minutes; by the time a refresh shows one it may be gone, and both bets must be placed before either price moves.

None right now (184 quotes checked).

Hedging: middles

Over at a lower line at one book, under at a higher line at another. If the result lands in between, both win; if not, one wins and one loses (about the books' margin). Between is the chance it lands there, from the books' consensus curve; EV is the expected profit per unit staked. Not guaranteed. Only positive ones are shown.

None with positive expected profit right now.

Game lines: spreads, moneylines, totals

The same check on the main markets. Each book's price against the other books' read; a spread or total at a different number is priced on how often NFL games end on each margin and total (since 1999) -- half a point around 3 or 7 is worth far more than elsewhere. Wins is the chance the bet wins at that number (a push returns the stake). No opinion of ours on who wins: main lines are the sharpest market there is, so expect few. Long-shot moneylines (under a 15% chance) are left out: the books' read overstates them.

These prices were read Wed 4:50 AM ET (6h before this page was built); the feed is re-read every few hours, not every refresh.

None right now: no spread, moneyline or total beats what the other books say by 2%+ (24 quotes on 15 games checked).

Record: 12 flagged, 2-4, -2.1 units at one a bet.

Not advice: an edge on paper is a fraction of a percent to a few percent, and a long losing stretch is normal. The record above is the test of whether these flags are worth acting on.

Each player's future is simulated (role drift, injuries, byes, the next man up taking over -- graded on 2022-2025 seasons it was not fitted to: points per game land in its middle half half the time, early form carries on as far as it really did, and what a manager can see of a player moves as much, and means as little, as a real projection did); every team starts its best lineup each week on what it could see then; the season is played on the real schedule and the playoffs on the real bracket. Rosters are held as they stand. The small ranges are 95% intervals for the simulation's own noise (Wilson): what a rerun could move the number by -- not whether the model's view of the season is right. Power is record-blind: the share of the other teams' scores a team beats in an average remaining week (all-play), from the same simulation and the same fading of team strength, so a team with a bad record and a strong roster ranks high here while its title odds stay low. Pts/wk ahead is the expected points a week for the rest of the regular season (a little closer together than raw projections: managers' waiver moves level rosters), so far what the team has scored a week in the weeks counted; a big gap between the two means the roster has changed or the points came on luck. Where this week's projections come from

Each player's number blends, where he has one from each:

  • our model and Yahoo's projection, 28% and 72%, measured on 946 graded games;
  • the betting market's implied points, 32% where books price him -- none in this week's numbers yet: books post a game's props a day or two before kickoff, the Sunday-morning run buys them, and a refresh spends no credits, so it uses only props already bought;
  • the FantasyPros consensus projection, 13% (9 of your 13 players), measured on 1676 graded games.

Each weight is the one that would have been most accurate on this season's finished games, pulled toward its starting value until enough are graded. The same numbers set the lineup, P(win), this week's pickups and streams, and this week's part of every title-odds number on the page: waiver adds and drops, trades, the roster. Season values move 55% of the way toward the FantasyPros rest-of-season consensus (measured on 1423 graded games), and every season-long number uses them.

Waiver moves, by title odds

Waiver plans: several moves together

Moves interact -- two backs chasing one lineup spot are worth less together, two dead roster spots turned into a starter and his handcuff can be worth more -- so every combination of two or three pickups and drops is screened, and the best priced in title odds against standing pat and against the best single move. Make the plan when it beats that single move by more than the simulation noise; a close call when by less.

Most valuable players

Value is points above a waiver pickup at his position, summed over weeks 10-17: what he is simulated to score each week he plays, less what the pickup would. Weeks he misses (byes, injuries, a reported timeline) count nothing, so a hurt star drops down. Upside is that value in his best tenth of simulated seasons: a breakout, a bigger role, a clean bill of health. Pickup level a game: QB 17.3, RB 6.6, WR 8.0, TE 8.0, K 10.7, D/ST 8.5. RoS/g is his season value a game and Δwk its move since last week (green up, red down, yellow flat; deeper is bigger -- tap Δwk for the risers, again for the fallers), Wk this week's projection, G games expected, Range his points a week (10th-90th percentile) and Mkt what the rest of the league sees him worth a game (those three on wider screens). Tap a column to sort; your players are highlighted. Tap a player's name for his game log: points, snap share and stat line, week by week.

Betting

Prop lines that look wrong. For each player and stat, the other books' quotes (their margin taken out; Pinnacle, the sharpest, counts double) are fitted to one curve of his outcomes, so any line can be priced: a book at 30.5 rushing yards when the rest sit near 72 shows as a near-certain over. Ours is the chance from our own projection of that stat and how much such projections miss by (2021-2025). Combined leans toward the books on yards (they know the matchup) and toward ours where we have been as good. EV is the expected profit per unit staked at that price: on the books' chance, and on the combined one. Way off: 10%+ on both the books' read and ours. One-sided markets (anytime touchdown) are left out.

Built Wed 10:29 AM ET. Age is how long before that each price was last read from its feed: the feeds are re-read every few hours (one of them mostly on Sunday, Tuesday and Wednesday mornings), not every refresh, and a price more than 90 minutes behind the newest for the same player, or more than 8 hours old, is left out as stale. Props move fast, so check the book before betting. Books limit accounts that keep taking prices well off the market.

Recommended: prices the other books say are wrong

Each one pays more than the other books' read says it should, and more than the combined read does: positive expected profit if the other books are right and the price is still there. Whether that has held is the record below (wins and losses, and whether the market then moved toward these bets or away from them); until it does, keep stakes small. Even a real edge loses most single bets.

None right now: no price beats what the other books say by 2%+ (14 sides priced). Lines that are way off are rare and get fixed fast; the board checks every refresh.

The close is the early test of an edge: a real one beats the closing price more often than not, and the market moves toward it. Parlays

Two or three of the recommended bets above, at the same book and from different games (so they don't move together). A parlay pays the legs' odds multiplied and wins only if all do, so a parlay of good prices multiplies the edge — and the error in the chances, and the book's margin on any leg that isn't an edge. It wins far less often, so keep the stake smaller than a single bet's. Legs avg is what the same legs earn as separate bets.

None right now: it needs two recommended bets at one book from different games.

Hedging: sure bets

The same line at two books, over at one and under at the other, where the two prices together pay more than the stakes whichever way it lands. Stake the split shown. They are rare and corrected in minutes; by the time a refresh shows one it may be gone, and both bets must be placed before either price moves.

None right now (184 quotes checked).

Hedging: middles

Over at a lower line at one book, under at a higher line at another. If the result lands in between, both win; if not, one wins and one loses (about the books' margin). Between is the chance it lands there, from the books' consensus curve; EV is the expected profit per unit staked. Not guaranteed. Only positive ones are shown.

None with positive expected profit right now.

Game lines: spreads, moneylines, totals

The same check on the main markets. Each book's price against the other books' read; a spread or total at a different number is priced on how often NFL games end on each margin and total (since 1999) -- half a point around 3 or 7 is worth far more than elsewhere. Wins is the chance the bet wins at that number (a push returns the stake). No opinion of ours on who wins: main lines are the sharpest market there is, so expect few. Long-shot moneylines (under a 15% chance) are left out: the books' read overstates them.

These prices were read Wed 4:50 AM ET (6h before this page was built); the feed is re-read every few hours, not every refresh.

None right now: no spread, moneyline or total beats what the other books say by 2%+ (24 quotes on 15 games checked).

Record: 12 flagged, 2-4, -2.1 units at one a bet.

Not advice: an edge on paper is a fraction of a percent to a few percent, and a long losing stretch is normal. The record above is the test of whether these flags are worth acting on.

Each player's future is simulated (role drift, injuries, byes, the next man up taking over -- graded on 2022-2025 seasons it was not fitted to: points per game land in its middle half half the time, early form carries on as far as it really did, and what a manager can see of a player moves as much, and means as little, as a real projection did); every team starts its best lineup each week on what it could see then; the season is played on the real schedule and the playoffs on the real bracket. Rosters are held as they stand. The small ranges are 95% intervals for the simulation's own noise (Wilson): what a rerun could move the number by -- not whether the model's view of the season is right. Power is record-blind: the share of the other teams' scores a team beats in an average remaining week (all-play), from the same simulation and the same fading of team strength, so a team with a bad record and a strong roster ranks high here while its title odds stay low. Pts/wk ahead is the expected points a week for the rest of the regular season (a little closer together than raw projections: managers' waiver moves level rosters), so far what the team has scored a week in the weeks counted; a big gap between the two means the roster has changed or the points came on luck. Tap a column heading to sort.
